title: Square control: the whole board at once
outcomes: Reads the n-m counts and the blue or orange tint of the control map on any square
Names what the map leaves out: pins and x-rays
Glances at the map before moving, starting with the landing square

steps.text: Under a lesson board, the **Control map** button paints every square at once. Each square shows two numbers, **White-Black**: how many White pieces and how many Black pieces attack it. **Blue** means White's number is higher, **orange** means Black's. Tap any square to see which pieces they are. Counting attackers is taught in its own lessons; here you learn to read the picture.

steps.caption: White to move. Turn on the map and tap f7.

line.say: The knight joins the bishop. The map on f7 changes from 1-1 to 2-1.

steps.text: The map is a **rule-based count, not a verdict**. A blue square does not mean White wins a fight there; it only says White has more pieces looking at it. Two things it leaves out, on purpose: **pins** (a pinned piece still counts) and **x-rays** (a piece behind another piece does not count). Check both by eye.

steps.title: Same map, different truth
steps.prompt: Both boards show f3 as 0-1 with a black knight on e5. Only one rook has moved. Can the knight capture on f3? Predict first, then check.

steps.text: Make the map a **habit before you move**, in this order. First, the square you want to land on: is Black's number above zero? Second, your own pieces: any whose Black number is higher than yours? Third, a quick look for pins and pieces lined up behind others. It takes seconds and replaces a vague worry with two numbers.

steps.caption: White considers the knight jump to d4. What would the map say there?

line.say: On d4 the map would read 0-2: no White support, two Black attackers.
Black can take with the pawn.

steps.prompt: Which of the three limits of the map (pins, x-rays, 'a number is not a verdict') would you have forgotten? How will you remind yourself to check it?
